paragraphs.heading: What it studies
paragraphs.text: Gravitational-wave astronomy is the branch of astronomy that detects and studies gravitational waves coming from objects in space. Gravitational waves are tiny ripples in spacetime, set off when massive objects accelerate. Violent events produce them: pairs of black holes merging, neutron stars joining, supernova explosions, and processes in the early universe just after the Big Bang.

paragraphs.heading: Like light, but for gravity
paragraphs.text: Light, radio waves and X-rays carry energy as ripples in the electromagnetic field. Gravitational radiation is similar, but it ripples the relatively weaker gravitational field. The waves spread out from their source at the speed of light and carry energy with them. Newton's law of gravity has no room for them, because it assumes that gravity acts instantly, at infinite speed.

paragraphs.heading: From idea to detection
paragraphs.text: Oliver Heaviside suggested such waves in 1893, and Henri Poincaré did so in 1905. Albert Einstein predicted them in 1916 from general relativity, though later he refused to accept them. The first evidence came from the Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar, two neutron stars whose orbit decays just as expected if energy leaks away as gravitational radiation, and Hulse and Taylor won the 1993 Nobel Prize. A direct signal arrived only in 2015, when LIGO's detectors in Louisiana and Washington caught two black holes merging, and the 2017 Nobel Prize went to Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne and Barry Barish.

paragraphs.heading: How the detectors work
paragraphs.text: Today's detectors use laser interferometry: they measure tiny changes in the length of two arms set at right angles as a wave passes through. These instruments stretch for kilometres and include the two LIGO detectors in the United States, Virgo in Italy, GEO600 in Germany and KAGRA in Japan. LIGO, Virgo and KAGRA have observed together, while GEO600 is less sensitive and mostly used for trial runs. When three or more detectors catch the same event, the small delays between them show where in the sky it came from.

paragraphs.heading: Seeing what light cannot
paragraphs.text: Light from distant objects is scattered, absorbed, reflected and bent along the way, so information gets lost. Some regions, such as the insides of nebulae, thick dust at the galaxy's core and the surroundings of black holes, let photons through only partly. Gravitational waves can be used alongside light to study the universe in finer detail. Joining gravitational-wave data with data from other wavelengths, to get a fuller picture, is called multi-messenger astronomy.

paragraphs.heading: Hard problems and next steps
paragraphs.text: The field can help probe the early universe, test theories of gravity and reveal how dark matter and dark energy are spread out. It may also help pin down the Hubble constant, which describes how fast the universe is expanding. Its problems include noise, a lack of ultra-sensitive instruments and trouble catching low-frequency waves. On the ground, seismic shaking disturbs detectors, and the curve of Earth's surface limits how long their arms can be. Plans include better detectors and possibly ones in space, such as LISA, the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, which should pick up supermassive black holes, primordial black holes and merging pairs of white dwarfs.

paragraphs.heading: Listening with pulsars
paragraphs.text: Another way to listen uses pulsar timing arrays. Three groups, the European Pulsar Timing Array, NANOGrav in North America and the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array, work together as the International Pulsar Timing Array. They use radio telescopes that already exist. Because they are tuned to waves in the nanohertz range, finding a signal takes many years of watching, and their sensitivity improves only gradually.
